Name: Identify, assess, disclose, review, and mitigate sustainability impacts
Guideline: Assess and report the planet, people, and prosperity impacts of digital projects, and plan measurable reductions to the real-world effects of their activity.
Context: The catalog frames this broadly — spanning things like supply chain emissions and infrastructure effects, not just the product's own runtime footprint — and calls for public disclosure of the assessment, not just an internal one.

Name: Understand user requirements or constraints
Guideline: Identify and involve users and affected communities, and research their needs.
Context: The W3C guideline frames this as a waste-prevention step: without first understanding real user needs, device constraints, and connectivity limitations, teams risk building features nobody needs or that exclude users — both of which waste development and runtime resources.

Name: Integrate sustainability into every stage of the ideation process
Guideline: Design and review sustainable branding and experiences, involve users throughout the process, and reduce unnecessary development and environmental impact through early testing and environmentally aware design.
Context: The catalog's concrete technique: use wireframes and rapid prototypes to test ideas early, and consider adopting a “planet-focused persona” alongside user personas during ideation, so environmental constraints get a seat at the table from the start.

Name: Design efficient and streamlined user journeys
Guideline: Design clear, efficient journeys that help users complete tasks and find content with minimal effort.
Context: The catalog breaks this into three concrete moves: streamline task completion by cutting unnecessary steps, reuse design patterns users already recognize instead of novel ones, and make content findable through sitemaps, navigation, and search rather than requiring users to hunt.

Name: Design to assist and not to distract
Guideline: Give users control over notifications and focus, prioritize task-relevant content, and avoid designs that distract or unnecessarily extend engagement.
Context: The catalog names the specific anti-pattern it's targeting: engagement traps like infinite scroll, which it says should be avoided in favor of keeping disruptive or attention-extending elements optional rather than default.

Name: Avoid being manipulative or deceptive
Guideline: Avoid deceptive patterns, clearly label ads, respect consent for tracking, and ensure search, sharing, and discoverability practices prioritize user needs over optimization or manipulation.
Context: The catalog names specific tactics to avoid — bait-and-switch and fake scarcity are called out explicitly — alongside the more general instruction to keep advertising honest and search-optimization genuinely user-serving rather than algorithm-gaming.

Name: Make deliverables understandable and reusable
Guideline: Create discoverable, maintainable, and reusable documentation and code resources that support long-term understanding, reuse, and sustainability.
Context: The catalog's concrete pieces: keep source code commented and accessible (not just the documentation), and have an actual process for updating or retiring outdated information rather than letting it accumulate indefinitely.

Name: Use a design system for interface consistency
Guideline: Use design systems and established patterns to ensure consistent, efficient, and sustainable interfaces through reusable components and clear maintenance practices.
Context: The catalog adds a specific technical point beyond just consistency: load only the components a given page actually needs rather than the whole system, and it notes the sustainability payoff compounds most for large teams, where clear component ownership cuts down on duplicated one-off assets.

Name: Optimize media to reduce resource use
Guideline: Include media only when it supports user needs. Manage, optimize, and load media efficiently. Ensure users have control over playback and data use.
Context: The catalog's concrete implementation: lazy-load media so it's only fetched when it's about to be seen, disable autoplay by default rather than opt-out, and be transparent with users about how much data a piece of media will use before they load it.

Name: Ensure animation is proportionate and easy to control
Guideline: Use animation sparingly and efficiently, only when it supports understanding, while limiting performance impact and giving users control over motion.
Context: The catalog's specific technical recommendation: implement animation using efficient, native browser capabilities rather than heavier custom/JS-driven approaches, since the implementation method itself can be as significant to resource cost as whether to animate at all.

Name: Use optimized web typography
Guideline: Use font strategies that minimize downloads and complexity while supporting required languages and dynamic content.
Context: The catalog's concrete techniques: prefer system fonts where possible, limit how many custom fonts get downloaded, subset character sets to just what the content actually uses, and provide fallback fonts so readability doesn't depend on a slow download completing.

Name: Avoid unwanted notifications
Guideline: Send only user-requested notifications and provide clear, accessible controls for managing preferences, opt-in, and account and contact settings.
Context: The catalog is specific about the default state: optional notifications should ship disabled by default, requiring an explicit opt-in, rather than being on until a user finds the settings to turn them off.

Name: Reduce the impact of downloadable and physical documents
Guideline: Reduce paper use through digital-first workflows, optimize and reuse accessible downloadable documents, and provide clear, user-controlled document previews and formats.
Context: The catalog's specific transparency requirement: show users a file's size, format, and language options before they download it, so the choice to download a smaller or more appropriate version is actually available to them, not just theoretically possible.

Name: Involve users early in the project
Guideline: Define and validate prototypes and interface components through user testing to ensure they work effectively in real-world use cases and across diverse user needs.
Context: The catalog frames the timing as the point: validating with representative users during development, rather than after launch, is what avoids shipping a design that then needs resource-costly rework once real usage reveals the problem.

Name: Audit and test for bugs or issues requiring resolution
Guideline: Regularly audit for issues or problems, running tests at regular intervals in both simulated and real-world scenarios to ensure stability of the project.
Context: The catalog distinguishes two complementary channels: automated tests catch issues before release, while real-world monitoring catches the ones that only show up under actual production conditions — both feeding into finding bottlenecks in either the code or the infrastructure.

Name: Validate usability through testing and real-world usage
Guideline: Monitor user feedback and real usage to evaluate feature effectiveness, and use usability testing and user research to guide ongoing improvements.
Context: The catalog adds a concrete signal beyond usability testing and interviews: tracking a feature's actual adoption rate after release, since a feature nobody ends up using is a resource cost with no offsetting user value, regardless of how well it tested beforehand.

Name: Provide cross-platform compatibility support
Guideline: Document compatibility, avoid unnecessary obsolescence, and test across devices, systems, and network conditions.
Context: The catalog frames the payoff directly in e-waste terms: maintaining broad compatibility — tested against slow connections, older devices, and different operating systems — is what avoids forcing users into a premature device replacement just to keep using the product.

Name: Set goals based on performance and energy impact
Guideline: Define performance and environmental targets, and design content with awareness of the relative energy and processing cost.
Context: The catalog's underlying test: complex structures, heavy graphics, and script-driven experiences all consume more computational resources than simpler alternatives, so the guideline's bar is that this extra cost has to be justified by genuine value to the user, not just visual polish.

Name: Minify and remove unused code
Guideline: Minify code and data, and remove unused characters to reduce file size and improve loading efficiency and maintainability.
Context: The catalog calls out dead CSS and JavaScript specifically as the common target, and adds a caution worth keeping in mind: verify minification doesn't silently break something, since a broken minified bundle forcing a fallback reload would defeat the whole point.

Name: Modularize bandwidth-heavy components
Guideline: Split large components into smaller, on-demand modules to improve loading efficiency while balancing maintainability and caching performance.
Context: The catalog adds an important caveat the base guideline doesn't: splitting too aggressively into many tiny modules can backfire, since excessive fragmentation increases request overhead and undermines caching effectiveness — the goal is balanced code-splitting, not maximum fragmentation.

Name: Avoid redundancy and duplication in code
Guideline: Reduce code duplication through refactoring and reuse, ensure maintainability, and favor evolving existing solutions over rebuilding them.
Context: The catalog's default bias is toward evolution over replacement: improve an existing implementation rather than rebuild it from scratch, unless the rebuild would clearly and specifically improve performance or user experience — rebuilding by default is treated as the wasteful option.

Name: Treat third parties the same as first parties
Guideline: Minimize and carefully manage third-party services by using lightweight, user-controlled integrations that are loaded only when needed.
Context: The catalog adds two concrete techniques and a requirement: lazy-load third-party content only on user interaction rather than by default, self-host assets where feasible instead of pulling from an external CDN, and hold any third party to the same security/privacy bar as the site owner itself, not a looser one.

Name: Ensure code follows good semantic practices
Guideline: Use standards-compliant HTML and web platform features, and avoid unnecessary complexity or non-standard code.
Context: The catalog's specific test for what to cut: remove optional elements that don't actually improve usability or accessibility, and treat deprecated or proprietary technology as something that needs active justification to keep, not a default that stays until someone objects.

Name: Defer the loading of non-critical resources
Guideline: Load non-essential assets asynchronously or with prioritization to improve rendering performance and avoid visual issues.
Context: The catalog names the specific visual failure modes this prevents — Flash Of Unstyled Content (FOUC), Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT), and Flash of Faux Text (FOFT) — which is what deferred, prioritized loading is actually protecting against, beyond just raw speed.

Name: Structure metadata for machine readability
Guideline: Include essential document metadata and structured data to improve usability, accessibility, and machine readability.
Context: The catalog's concrete example is structured data via schema.org/JSON-LD, and it explicitly extends the audience for this beyond browsers and search engines to AI tools too — the same markup that helps search rankings also helps automated systems interpret the page correctly instead of guessing.

Name: Use media queries that support sustainability goals
Guideline: Support user preferences via media queries for color, motion, contrast, data use, and related settings to improve accessibility and efficiency.
Context: The catalog names the specific CSS media features this is about: `prefers-color-scheme` and `prefers-reduced-data` are the two it calls out explicitly, letting the site adapt its rendering cost to settings the user already configured at the OS or browser level.

Name: Ensure layouts work for different devices and requirements
Guideline: Use responsive, progressively enhanced, and carbon-aware design to ensure accessible, adaptable functionality across devices and interaction methods while managing resource use.
Context: The catalog's concrete carbon-aware technique: temporarily disable non-essential features during periods of high electricity demand or system load, as long as this is done transparently so users understand why something is unavailable rather than assuming it's broken.

Name: Use sustainable JavaScript and APIs
Guideline: Write efficient JavaScript and use APIs that minimize processing, data use, and energy consumption.
Context: The W3C guideline gets specific here: reduce unnecessary calculations and DOM updates, and use browser APIs like Compression Streams or Page Visibility deliberately, so client-side code isn’t burning energy for work the user doesn’t need.

Name: Use dependencies sparingly and maintain them
Guideline: Regularly review dependencies, remove unused or unnecessary libraries and frameworks, and keep required packages up to date. Opt for minimal, secure, and modular solutions.
Context: The catalog frames this as an ongoing audit practice, not a one-time cleanup: regularly re-check for unused packages, and lean toward established, trusted libraries over rolling a custom implementation, since a trusted dependency is usually the safer bet on both security and maintenance burden.

Name: Include expected and beneficial files
Guideline: Include standard website metadata and configuration files to support discoverability, transparency, and operational best practices.
Context: The catalog gives a concrete checklist, split into two tiers: “expected” files like favicon.ico, robots.txt, site.webmanifest, and sitemap.xml, plus “beneficial” ones like carbon.txt, security.txt, and humans.txt that go further on transparency and trust.

Name: Use the most efficient solution for your service
Guideline: Choose lightweight, efficient implementation approaches that balance effort, performance, and environmental impact while favoring simple, native, and static solutions.
Context: The catalog adds an ongoing-maintenance angle beyond the initial choice: regularly re-review any third-party components you did pull in, since a dependency that was the efficient choice when added can stop being the best option as alternatives evolve.

Name: Use the latest stable language version
Guideline: Use up-to-date technologies and select the most suitable programming language for each task to ensure efficiency and maintainability.
Context: The catalog's practical test for whether to adopt something newer: only justified when the efficiency or maintainability gain actually outweighs the cost of migrating, and the technology has enough community support to be a safe long-term bet — not simply because a newer version exists.

Name: Reduce the number and complexity of database queries
Guideline: Optimize database use by minimizing and scoping queries, reducing repeated requests, and applying data governance practices.
Context: The catalog's concrete techniques: reuse a query's results locally instead of re-querying for the same data, and apply data governance practices like TTL (time-to-live) expiry and data minimization so the database itself isn't holding more than it needs to.

Name: Use sustainable hosting
Guideline: Select and manage infrastructure using sustainability metrics, prioritizing low-carbon energy use and low-impact hosting and domain choices in selection, and extending hardware lifespan and minimising emissions in management.
Context: The catalog's concrete selection criterion: prioritize hosts that transparently report their own energy efficiency, renewable energy usage, and emissions data, rather than taking sustainability marketing claims at face value — and on the hardware side, favor suppliers explicitly committed to device longevity, patching, and repair options.

Name: Optimize caching and support offline access
Guideline: Use caching and offline capabilities to reduce network load, improve resilience, and balance performance with sustainability.
Context: The catalog splits this into two techniques by content type: server-side caching for dynamic content, client-side caching for stable resources, plus Progressive Web App patterns and Service Workers specifically so essential content stays available during a network interruption, not just faster when the network is fine.

Name: Reduce data transfer with compression
Guideline: Compress server responses and media files to reduce bandwidth, storage use, and delivery overhead while balancing processing costs.
Context: The catalog adds a caution the base guideline doesn't state: avoid redundantly re-compressing files that are already optimized (like most image/video formats), since the processing cost of compressing something that won't shrink further is itself a waste to weigh against the bandwidth savings.

Name: Setup necessary error pages and redirection links
Guideline: Provide clear error handling and ensure broken links are either fixed or redirected to destinations to prevent navigation issues.
Context: The catalog's specific caution: avoid chaining multiple redirects together, since each hop adds a request the browser has to follow — a direct fix or a single redirect is the sustainability-conscious choice over a redirect pointing to another redirect.

Name: Avoid maintaining unnecessary virtualized environments or containers
Guideline: Remove unnecessary virtualized environments to improve efficiency and maintainability.
Context: The W3C guideline is about environment sprawl specifically: periodically deactivate or remove virtual machines and containers that are no longer in active use, since each idle environment still carries infrastructure and energy overhead even when nothing is running on it.

Name: Use automation wisely
Guideline: Automate and scale tasks and infrastructure efficiently, run processes only when needed, and control unwanted traffic.
Context: The catalog's concrete mechanism is CI/CD for recurring tasks, paired with choosing lower-impact tooling and scaling infrastructure to avoid overprovisioning — and it specifically calls out restricting unwanted bot/scraper traffic while still preserving access for legitimate users and search engine crawlers.

Name: Define the frequency of data refreshes
Guideline: Decide when to refresh data based on a balance of user and sustainability requirements.
Context: The W3C guideline frames this as a caching decision: set data/cache refresh intervals based on how current the data actually needs to be for users, rather than defaulting to frequent refreshes that burn compute and network resources without a real accuracy benefit.

Name: Back up critical data at routine intervals
Guideline: Back up data at regular intervals to ensure that there are failsafes that can be relied upon should an issue occur.
Context: The catalog's specific quality bar for the backups themselves: they should be incremental (to minimize the storage and time cost of each backup) as well as secure, and access to sensitive information within a backup should be limited just like it would be in the live system.

Name: Assess the impact and requirements of data processing
Guideline: Use carbon-aware scheduling, efficient and secure protocols, and simple system designs to reduce unnecessary processing while balancing performance, security, and constraints.
Context: The catalog's concrete pieces: schedule compute-heavy tasks for periods of lower grid carbon intensity, prefer modern protocols like HTTP/3 over legacy ones, and decide whether a given task should run client-side or server-side based on which is actually more sustainable overall, not just which is more convenient to implement.

Name: Use Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) when beneficial
Guideline: Use CDNs and data location strategically for static content and processing only when they improve efficiency and sustainability, while avoiding unnecessary distribution and transfers.
Context: The catalog's specific caution: putting dynamic or frequently-changing resources on a CDN can backfire, since browser security mechanisms can undermine the caching benefit that's the entire point of using a CDN in the first place — reserve CDNs for genuinely static content.

Name: Ensure infrastructure fits project requirements
Guideline: Use demand-matched, autoscaling infrastructure to meet demand efficiently without overprovisioning.
Context: The W3C guideline is essentially rightsizing for infrastructure: use demand-matched, autoscaling resources sized for typical usage patterns rather than provisioning for peak-case scenarios that sit mostly idle.

Name: Store data according to the needs of your users
Guideline: Regularly manage and reduce stored data (including content, logs, media, and downloads) using retention, compression, and lifecycle policies, while maintaining efficient access to long-term assets.
Context: The catalog adds two specific techniques beyond general lifecycle policies: optimize logging itself (not just application data) as a storage-reduction target, and enable direct asset downloads where possible so redundant requests don't have to keep passing back through the server.

Name: Have an ethical and sustainable product strategy
Guideline: Implement organizational practices around ethics, sustainability, and responsible data use. Publish and maintain policies that demonstrate their implementation.
Context: The catalog's concrete examples of what “policies” means here: a code of ethics, product guidelines, and a cloud sustainability strategy specifically, published in a dedicated sustainability section that's kept current — not just a one-time announcement.

Name: Assign a sustainability advocate
Guideline: Appoint a sustainability advocate who is provided with what they require to speak about and for issues relating to sustainability.
Context: The catalog suggests this role doesn't have to stay a single person: expanding it into a broader climate working group is called out as a way to amplify impact through collective effort, once the initial advocate role is established.

Name: Inform, raise awareness, and train for sustainability
Guideline: Provide ongoing training, onboarding, and guidance on sustainability practices, and support participation in sustainability initiatives through clear materials, knowledge sharing, and organizational encouragement.
Context: The catalog frames this as building organizational capacity, not a one-off session: ongoing training and knowledge-sharing aimed at everyone involved in a project — not just permanent staff — so sustainability practice doesn't depend on a single trained individual.

Name: Communicate the environmental impact of user choices
Guideline: Empower users, allowing them to make decisions when their choices can influence the environmental impact they have.
Context: The catalog's specific mechanism: show users a quantified sense of how their actions affect energy use, emissions, or resource consumption — not just a general sustainability statement — so the informed choice it's asking for is actually possible to make.

Name: Calculate the environmental impact
Guideline: Assess and compare full life cycle environmental impacts, including those of third-party services, to inform sustainable design decisions.
Context: The catalog adds a comparative dimension beyond an internal audit: evaluate how your solution's life-cycle impact stacks up against competitors' as part of the assessment, not just measure your own footprint in isolation.

Name: Define clear organizational sustainability goals and metrics
Guideline: Define measurable sustainability goals and metrics, and communicate progress over time.
Context: The W3C guideline calls for concrete, measurable sustainability targets and metrics tracked over time — not just a general commitment — so progress (or the lack of it) can actually be reviewed and acted on.

Name: Validate web sustainability efforts through external verification
Guideline: Use independent verification to support and improve sustainability claims.
Context: The W3C guideline is about credibility: have sustainability claims checked by an independent third party (e.g. a life-cycle assessment or ESG audit) rather than self-reporting only, and revisit that verification periodically as practices change.

Name: Support mandatory disclosures and reporting
Guideline: Publish transparent, standards-aligned sustainability reports that track progress over time and clearly explain real impact reductions without misleading reporting.
Context: The catalog is specific about cadence and honesty: an annual impact report is the expectation, and it explicitly names greenwashing and selective data reporting as the failure modes this guideline is meant to rule out, not just encourage transparency in the abstract.

Name: Create one or more impact business models
Guideline: Describe how revenue generation supports environmental and social outcomes.
Context: The W3C guideline goes further than a one-off CSR statement: document an explicit "theory of change" connecting how the organization actually makes money to the environmental/social outcomes it claims to support, and track progress against that connection over time.

Name: Follow a product management and maintenance strategy
Guideline: Maintain clear documentation, resourcing, and measurement practices for long-term product support, including security, sustainability, and early detection of failure risks.
Context: The catalog frames the real alternative this guideline is meant to prevent: a product being effectively abandoned because it was never given adequate staffing or budget to address technical debt and evolving needs, rather than being deliberately retired.

Name: Implement continuous improvement procedures
Guideline: Maintain continuous improvement processes that balance feature changes, maintenance, and updates with user value and sustainability outcomes.
Context: The catalog gives four explicit criteria for keep/modify/add/remove decisions on any feature: environmental impact, user value, actual usage, and maintenance cost — and it specifically frames eliminating unused features as part of the process, not just adding new ones.

Name: Document updates and evolutions
Guideline: Provide documentation to help users find their way whenever functionality changes.
Context: The W3C guideline is about change communication: keep clear, structured documentation and version history so users understand what changed and why whenever a feature is added, modified, or removed — reducing confused re-work and support overhead on both sides.

Name: Evaluate if a digital product or service is necessary
Guideline: Assess alignment with sustainability goals, validate product need, and reduce barriers to access, usability, and fairness.
Context: The catalog's specific framework: validate genuine need using the desirability/feasibility/viability test, and check alignment against the UN Sustainable Development Goals specifically, rather than a generic “is this a good idea” assessment.

Name: Provide a supplier standards of practice document
Guideline: Select and work with suppliers based on sustainability principles, measure their impact, and transparently publish partnership outcomes.
Context: The catalog is explicit that this doesn't stop at internal measurement: publicly disclosing both the supplier partnership and its combined sustainability impact results is treated as part of the requirement, not an optional extra step.

Name: Share economic benefits
Guideline: Commit to fair pay, align workers and contractors with shared impact goals, and provide employee benefits within available resources.
Context: The catalog names living wages specifically as the fair-pay bar, and is pragmatic about benefits — tailored to what an organization can actually afford, rather than a fixed universal package, so this stays achievable for smaller teams too.

Name: Share decision-making power with affected parties
Guideline: Involve users and staff in decision-making, ensure human oversight, and provide transparency, and create challenge mechanisms for automated decisions.
Context: The catalog's trigger condition is specific: this is really about automated decision-making systems in particular — whenever software is making a decision that affects someone, human oversight and a way to challenge that outcome need to exist, not just for major organizational choices.

Name: Use Diversity, Equity, Justice, Inclusion (DEJI) practices
Guideline: Publish and act on Diversity, Equity, Justice, Inclusion (DEJI) and accessibility commitments, support training and measurable progress, and ensure inclusive outcomes across products and operations.
Context: The catalog names concrete training topics — algorithmic bias and the digital divide specifically — and concrete areas to track measurable progress against: hiring, leadership representation, and day-to-day operations, not just a general diversity statement.

Name: Promote responsible data practices
Guideline: Respect user data rights and manage data lifecycle through minimized collection, user control, portability, deletion, and content archiving.
Context: The catalog adds an automation angle: regularly archiving or removing outdated content should happen through automated processes rather than relying on manual review to remember, since manual cleanup is exactly the kind of task that tends to get deprioritized indefinitely.

Name: Establish responsible practices around AI and emerging or disruptive technologies
Guideline: Ensure responsible use of automated systems by only using ethically sourced and suitably sized data and models, managing environmental impacts, supporting workforce adaptation, respecting user agent controls, and using post-quantum encryption only where justified.
Context: The catalog puts a need-assessment step before any technical requirement: evaluate whether the AI/emerging-tech deployment is actually necessary at all before implementing it, since an unnecessary model is wasted resource consumption regardless of how ethically its data was sourced.

Name: Adopt responsible financial practices
Guideline: Adopt responsible financing practices by divesting from high-carbon assets and aligning budgeting and financial partnerships with long-term sustainability.
Context: The catalog's concrete example goes beyond just divesting from fossil fuels: it also calls for redirecting the organization's own banking relationships toward environmentally responsible financial partners, treating where an organization banks as itself a sustainability decision.

Name: Adopt organizational philanthropy practices
Guideline: Align partnerships and corporate giving with the organization's purpose, and support skill-building voluntary and pro bono work through clear partnership and giving policies.
Context: The catalog frames this as a two-way benefit rather than pure charity: formal policies that let employees contribute professional skills to nonprofits are positioned as generating real learning and development for the employee too, alongside the community impact.

Name: Plan for a digital product or service's care and end-of-life
Guideline: Document when a project is shut down and make users aware of what will happen to their data.
Context: The catalog's success criteria are concrete: end-of-life documentation should specifically cover data disposal, archiving, and file deletion — treated as protecting user privacy and data security as much as it is about reducing e-waste.

Name: Repair, reuse, refurbish, recycle or reduce e-waste
Guideline: Prioritize repair, reuse, refurbishment, and responsible recycling of hardware and e-waste through certified services, including supporting users doing repairs.
Context: The catalog's ordering is explicit: prioritize reusing equipment the organization already has before purchasing anything new, and on the right-to-repair side specifically, that means making replacement parts and clear repair instructions available to the people who bought the product, not just a policy statement.

Name: Define performance, environmental, and human budgets
Guideline: Define and apply lifecycle sustainability and performance budgets, set evidence-based KPIs, and track measurable improvements over time.
Context: The catalog names a third budget type the base guideline doesn't spell out: alongside environmental and performance (data transfer/file size) budgets, it also calls for a “human budget” protecting developer wellbeing — treating burnout as a sustainability metric worth tracking too.

Name: Use and contribute to open source
Guideline: Define and maintain an open-source policy and actively contribute to open-source communities through code, time, and financial or in-kind support.
Context: The catalog's stated rationale is specific: participating in open source — through code, funding, or volunteer time — reduces duplication of effort industry-wide, since shared, well-maintained tools mean fewer organizations independently reinventing the same thing.

Name: Create a business continuity and disaster recovery plan
Guideline: Maintain tested incident response plans and communicate transparently with users about service issues, risks, and recovery.
Context: The catalog is specific that transparency during an incident includes potential data risks, not just service-availability status — users should be told if their data might have been affected, not just when the service will be back up.
